Please be advised that the north gate will be closed on Saturday 18 April from 9 am to 2 pm while repairs are carried out on a leaking water pipe near the entrance. During this time, all visitors should use the east entrance to access the garden.

Because of the repair work, the seed swap originally planned for Saturday will now take place on Sunday at 11 am. Please bring any clearly labelled seeds you would like to share, and feel free to come along even if you do not have seeds to contribute.

Volunteers helping with the repair area and general tidy-up on Saturday should bring their own gloves. All tools will be supplied by the garden, so there is no need to bring spades, cutters, or other equipment.

Mina will be coordinating volunteers on the day and will meet helpers by the east entrance at 9 am. Thank you for your patience and support while we make this necessary repair and keep the garden safe and welcoming for everyone.

I picked this grinder up secondhand from a neighbor, and after two weeks I have mixed feelings. The fine settings are excellent. My espresso shots came out consistent, with a lovely crema I didn't expect from a used machine. The coarse settings are another story. When I tried French press, the grounds were noticeably uneven, with chunky bits mixed in alongside fine dust, which made the coffee muddy.

The motor is also loud enough to wake my whole household before 7 a.m. On the plus side, the removable cup makes cleanup simple. I just pop it out, rinse it, and I'm done. Worth buying if you drink mostly espresso.

At 3:40 a.m., while the second batch of rye proofed, Marisol found it again: a library book on the flour bin by the back door, its plastic jacket cold from the alley.

Fourth Thursday running. Same book, *A Field Guide to Night Birds*, Eastgate Branch, with a fresh due-date slip every time. She'd dropped it in the return box on her way home each week, and by the following Thursday someone had checked it out again and carried it back here.

She scraped dough from her knuckles and opened it. A folded index card slid out from the page on barn owls, where someone had penciled a check beside *call: a long, harsh scream*.

*You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until five. I walk my mother's dog at half past three, because she can't anymore. Heard one of these behind the dumpster. I keep checking this out again. —R.*

Marisol read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside, the fan rattled steam across the wet dumpster lid.

She turned the card over. With the grease pencil she used for marking trays, she wrote: *Rye's out at 4:15.* Then she wrapped a heel from yesterday's loaf in wax paper, set it on the outside step, laid the book on top, and propped the back door open one inch.

text:
Two properties are in play, and they pull in different directions. Conductivity is how fast heat moves through the metal. Heat capacity is how much heat the metal holds at a given temperature. Aluminum wins on the first. Cast iron wins on the second, mostly because a typical skillet is far heavier.

A 10-inch cast-iron skillet weighs around five pounds. A thin aluminum pan of the same width might weigh one. At the same temperature, the iron pan stores several times more heat, simply because there is more metal to store it in.

Now put a cold steak on each. The aluminum pan spreads heat evenly and quickly, but it has little in reserve. The steak pulls heat out, the pan's surface temperature drops, and the burner has to catch up. The iron pan's surface dips less, because the thick body keeps feeding heat to the steak. That is why the sear stays hard and the crust browns instead of the meat turning gray and steaming.

The limitation: cast iron conducts poorly, so it heats unevenly. A small burner leaves a hot spot under the flame and cooler edges. Staying hot is not the same as heating evenly.
